faqs.q: Pocket gophers are tearing up our Dade City pasture edge — what are they?
faqs.a: Southeastern pocket gophers: solitary, burrowing rodents that push fan-shaped sand mounds while tunneling for roots, common in Pasco's sandy grove soils. They are distinct from moles (surface ridges) and from the protected gopher tortoise (one big half-moon burrow, hands off). Pocket gophers are lawful trapping work, quoted by the extent of the mound system after a walk — pasture edges and yards price by the system's size, not by the mound count alone.

Dade City.wildlife_intro:
Dade City is Pasco's county seat and its old soul — a historic downtown of antique shops on the hills, Pioneer Florida heritage, and surrounding cattle, citrus, and kumquat country (the Kumquat Festival is serious business). Rolling terrain for Florida, big oaks, and farm country in every direction. The wildlife is rural-county-seat complete: squirrels and raccoons in the historic homes, armadillos and pocket gophers in the sandy yards, bats in the old downtown buildings, and tortoises on the dry hills.

Dade City service is small-city complete: historic carpentry downtown, farm walks outside it. The kumquat and citrus groves keep rat populations fed, so grove-side homes get the fallen-fruit lecture with their sealing quote. Bat colonies in the antique district's buildings are surveyed at dusk and excluded in season — August 15 to April 15 — with summer work limited to preparation. Call (844) 544-3498; we run the county seat and the country around it together.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in New Port Richey?
faqs.a: New Port Richey pricing follows the river: cottage systems priced as crawl-plus-attic wholes, subdivision homes as packages — written after inspection in both cases.

faqs.q: What lives under our New Port Richey river cottage?
faqs.a: Usually an opossum, sometimes a skunk, occasionally an armadillo that dug in from the yard — the Cotee's cottages sit in perfect under-house habitat. We identify from the entry sign and any tracks in the river sand, fit one-way exits or trap, confirm empty, and skirt the cottage with a buried apron rated for wet ground. River cottages that get the full skirt generally end their under-house tenancy permanently; those that get a board nailed over one hole just teach the tenant to dig a second door.

New Port Richey.wildlife_intro:
New Port Richey fronts the Pithlachascotee River — the Cotee — where it meets the Gulf, with a historic downtown on the river, Sims Park, and neighborhoods running from the old riverfront east through subdivisions toward the US-19 sprawl. River and Gulf together: raccoons and roof rats in the older river neighborhoods, opossums under the raised river cottages, armadillos inland, and herons and manatees in the river itself as protected scenery. Port Richey across the river extends the pattern.

River-cottage work leads our New Port Richey list — crawl spaces, low attics, dock structures — with the subdivision sealing pattern east of town as the second craft. Downtown's older commercial buildings hold bat colonies handled in season. The Cotee's wildlife gets the referral respect: a bold alligator in the river goes to FWC, and our crews stay on the roofline side of the law and the ledger.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Wesley Chapel?
faqs.a: Wesley Chapel quotes are the new-community package: pattern gap-sealing priced after a confirmatory inspection, written per home, with preserve-edge hardening itemized where the lot demands it.

faqs.q: A tortoise burrow appeared in our new Wesley Chapel yard — we did not put it there?
faqs.a: The tortoise was there first — the ranchland your village replaced was gopher tortoise habitat, and surviving tortoises simply kept their burrows through construction where permits allowed, or moved in from the preserves. The burrow is protected: no filling, no blocking, a 25-foot buffer for projects, FWC permits for any relocation. Most Wesley Chapel owners coexist without incident — fence the dog's run away from the apron, mow around it, and the tenant pays rent in charm. We identify and mark burrows during inspections so the surprise happens once, on paper.

Wesley Chapel.wildlife_intro:
Wesley Chapel is Pasco's boomtown — master-planned communities like Seven Oaks, Meadow Pointe, and Wiregrass Ranch rising from cattle land along the SR-56 corridor, with the Shops at Wiregrass as its downtown. New-community wildlife is the whole story: everything the ranchland held — raccoons, armadillos, tortoises, coyotes — now meets brand-new rooflines full of builder gaps, and the ponds hold Muscovy ducks and the occasional gator within a year of filling.

Wesley Chapel is gap-audit country, and we say it plainly in every quote: the animals are not the anomaly, the unsealed new roofline is. Our inspections run the known production patterns, seal them as a package, and brief new Floridians on the tortoise burrow at the preserve edge and the crane pair at the pond. Association duck questions get the Control Order facts. The written quote follows the survey; the orientation is part of the visit.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Zephyrhills?
faqs.a: Zephyrhills pricing is seasonal-service honest: skirt work, full seals, and return assessments priced as distinct written jobs after inspection — the fall seal quoted as the complete job it needs to be.

faqs.q: We winter elsewhere — what should we do about our Zephyrhills home each spring before leaving?
faqs.a: Book the seal before you book the flight. We inspect the roofline, screens, skirting, and utility entries, seal everything a roof rat or raccoon uses, set the trash and fruit situation right, and photograph the finished work for your file. Homes that leave sealed come back clean; homes that leave with one open vent come back to a colony and a cleanup bill. Zephyrhills' summer vacancy is the longest in our service area, and it is exactly what the seal was invented for.

Zephyrhills.wildlife_intro:
Zephyrhills is the bottled-water town — springs country in Pasco's southeast, with a historic downtown, winter-visitor parks, and the Hillsborough River rising in the Green Swamp just east. Seasonal population swings define the wildlife calendar: winter residents arrive to find what the summer vacancy invited. Raccoons and roof rats in the empty-month homes, armadillos and moles in the yards, and along the river and the swamp edge, the full wet-country cast.

Pre-departure and return-arrival service is Zephyrhills' specialty in our practice: fall seals before the trip north, spring damage assessments on return. The mobile and park-model communities get skirt inspections as a standard line, because under those homes is where Zephyrhills animals actually live. River-edge properties get the property walk and the cottonmouth identification talk — the Hillsborough's headwater swamps hold them, along with far more harmless watersnakes.

faqs.q: Why are roof rats such a problem in Land O' Lakes?
faqs.a: Roof rats are Florida's main structure rat, and Land O' Lakes gives them exactly what they want: palm crowns, fruit trees, dense shrubs, and rooflines they can reach from fences and branches. They nest in attics and wall voids and breed year-round here. Our crew traps and excludes — sealing the entry and cutting back roof access — and frames structure work as nonchemical trapping and exclusion, because chemical rodent work in a structure is FDACS Chapter 482 pest-control territory.

Land O' Lakes.wildlife_intro:
In Land O' Lakes, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — southern Tampa suburbs, coastal communities, and rural lake and ranch country in the east — and features such as Withlacoochee River, Green Swamp, Anclote River, Werner-Boyce Salt Springs State Park keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Land O' Lakes jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

faqs.q: What should I do about armadillo digging in Hudson?
faqs.a: Nine-banded armadillos dig for grubs and earthworms in lawns and flower beds, and they are common throughout most of Florida, including Hudson. A live-trapped armadillo may be released on-site, or released within the same county on 40 or more contiguous acres with the landowner's written permission, within 24 hours — those are the Florida rules, and we follow them. We also talk through fencing and grub management, because trapping alone rarely ends digging in good habitat.
